The Stock Market Is "Petrified of Oracle's Balance Sheet" as Microsoft Walks Away ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle, days after Oracle canceled an estimated $7 billion chip-leasing deal with Tencent.

The Microsoft contract itself looks small, but losing it leaves Oracle's backlog leaning even harder on OpenAI, which S&P says accounts for about half of it.

Oracle's free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, its total debt reached $167 billion, and it sold another $20 billion of stock and notes on Nov. 2.

The market's fear looks justified until Oracle's mid-December results show its backlog growing with customers other than OpenAI.

Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) has stopped renewing a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) and is winding it down, Bloomberg reported on Friday. It's part of a wider review of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships.

That makes two AI deals Oracle has lost in a week. On Wednesday, Oracle canceled an estimated $7 billion chip-leasing deal with Tencent after pressure from the Trump administration, the Financial Times reported.

Investors were already nervous about the stock before either deal fell through. On Friday's weekly wrap of The Real Eisman Playbook, Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, talked about Oracle's new stock and bond sale:

"The market has become petrified of Oracle's balance sheet and its need for capital."

Microsoft just gave the market one more reason to be.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

A small contract from a very big customer

The deal goes back to 2023, when Oracle agreed to give Microsoft access to servers for an AI-assisted version of Bing. Microsoft has reportedly been switching that capacity off in recent months. The servers run on older-generation chips that no longer meet its specifications. The deal's full size couldn't be determined, and Oracle says demand for its AI infrastructure is still strong, including for older GPUs.

Oracle has some evidence for that. On its first-quarter call in September, management said capacity up for renewal was renewed or resold at a 20% premium, even though most of those GPUs were four years old or older. So the chips Microsoft hands back should find another renter. My guess is that this contract is a rounding error next to Oracle's backlog (the Tencent deal was about 1% of it).

Credo Technology Group Holding (CRDO) has contributed to the delivery of two new Open Compute Project optical telemetry standards, created with Oracle and industry partners. These standards aim to support more reliable AI data center networks by enabling richer link monitoring.

For investors watching Credo Technology Group Holding, the approval of these Open Compute Project standards lands after a sharp reset in sentiment. The share price has risen 7.3% over the last day but is still down 44.4% over 30 days, and the 1 year total shareholder return has declined 29.2%. However, the 3 year total shareholder return remains very strong at more than 7x, which points to fading near term momentum but a long runway of gains for early holders.

Credo Technology Group Holding has given back a large chunk of its multi year gains in just a few weeks. After that reset, is the bigger opportunity now ahead of investors, or already in the rear view mirror as valuation stands today?

Most Popular Narrative: 44% Undervalued

The fair value in the leading Credo Technology Group Holding narrative is $215 per share, which sits well above the last close at $120.51, pointing to a wide valuation gap that investors will want to understand.

That gap is central to the thesis from Womble, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, who argues that Credo Technology Group Holding needs to keep converting AI demand into high margin growth to justify a higher price.

Credo Technology Group is a high-growth semiconductor connectivity company benefiting from the expansion of AI infrastructure, data centres and high-speed optical and electrical networking. Q1 FY2027 revenue increased 114.7% year over year to $479.0 million, while Q2 revenue guidance of $525 to $535 million implies another approximately 9.6 to 11.7% sequential increase.

See why 25 investors see Credo Technology Group Holding as 44% undervalued.

Womble anchors the valuation on a personal fair value of $215 per share, paired with a future P/E assumption of about 57x and a high profit margin profile. That view leans heavily on the idea that revenue growth around the mid 20% range and non GAAP net margins near 49% can be sustained while AI infrastructure spending remains strong.

The same narrative flags clear break points that could challenge that optimism. These include revenue growth sliding below roughly 20%, non GAAP gross margin dropping under about 65%, or operating expenses starting to run faster than sales and eroding operating leverage.

At the same time, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock is up 6% to $49.18 after the company signed a multi-year cloud computing deal with British autonomous driving startup Wayve. Cloudflare's Best Quarter Ever Keeps the Rally Going

Cloudflare reported its Q3 2026 results after the close on November 5. The company's revenue rose 39.2% year over year (YoY) to $782.51 million, topping the $738.30 million consensus, according to Cloudflare's earnings release. On a per-share basis, Cloudflare's adjusted earnings of $0.38 beat the $0.3434 estimate.

CEO Matthew Prince called it "Cloudflare's best quarter ever" and credited "our fastest revenue growth in nearly four years, while expanding profitability." Management raised Cloudflare's full-year 2026 revenue outlook to $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion and guided its Q4 2026 revenue to $845 million to $846 million.

NVIDIA supplies the GPUs, networking gear and CUDA software that run most AI data centers. Last quarter, revenue rose 105.8% to $96.22 billion, and Data Center sales reached $89.02 billion. Two shocks caused the slide. First, Democrats won full control of Congress after running against unchecked data center expansion. Twelve Times Next Year's Earnings Prices in Almost No Growth

NVIDIA trades at about 20x fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $9.3124 and roughly 12x the fiscal 2028 estimate of $15.9146. Ninety days ago that fiscal 2028 figure stood at $12.8148, and analysts made zero downward revisions over the last 30 days.

The company has exceeded EPS estimates for six consecutive quarters. Most recently it posted $2.22 against a $2.09 consensus and guided third-quarter revenue to $108.0 billion. Vera Rubin is in full production at CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS). title: Microsoft Borrows at “10 Percentage Points Below CoreWeave.” Now It’s Backing Away From Neoclouds

Microsoft Borrows at "10 Percentage Points Below CoreWeave." Now It's Backing Away From Neoclouds ©@gorodenkoff from Getty Images via Canva, @DKosig from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Microsoft wants fewer neocloud partners and won't renew one of its cloud contracts with Oracle, CNBC reported on Friday.

Citi's Steven Wieting says Microsoft's cost of debt is about 10 percentage points below CoreWeave's. That makes owning data centers much cheaper for Microsoft than renting them.

Owning still costs a lot. Microsoft's capex reached $116 billion in fiscal 2026, and analysts expect its free cash flow to fall to $32.7 billion in fiscal 2027.

CoreWeave has the most to lose, and its results in the coming days will show how much it depends on Microsoft.

Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) helped create the neocloud boom. Now it's backing away from it, and CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) stand to lose business.

On Friday, CNBC's Seema Modi reported on Closing Bell Overtime that Microsoft has decided not to renew one of its cloud contracts with Oracle. Her sources also said Microsoft "is actively looking at shrinking the number of neoclouds it partners with as it doubles down on its own data center strategy."

On the same show, Citi's Steven Wieting put a number on Microsoft's edge. Its cost of debt, he said, "is about 10 percentage points below CoreWeave."

That's an enormous head start.

Microsoft pays its own way

Owning data centers isn't cheap. Analysts expect Microsoft's free cash flow to fall to $32.7 billion in fiscal 2027 (the year to June 2027). That's less than half the $67.0 billion it generated in fiscal 2026:

Microsoft (MSFT): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to June) (TIKR)

Analysts expect fiscal 2027 to be the low point, with free cash flow recovering to $47.0 billion in fiscal 2028. Capex is what's eating the cash. It climbed almost fivefold in four years, from $23.9 billion in fiscal 2022 to $116 billion in fiscal 2026:

Microsoft (MSFT): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2022-2026 (years to June) (TIKR)

Still, Microsoft pays for that building out of its own operations. In the September quarter, it was the only one of the five biggest AI spenders with positive free cash flow. At June 30, it held $76.8 billion of cash and short-term investments against $40.3 billion of debt.

Ten points adds up fast

CoreWeave is in a very different spot, since it borrows to build. Its total debt climbed from $6.28 billion at the end of September 2024 to $51.6 billion at the end of June 2026:

CoreWeave (CRWV): total debt, $ billions, last 8 quarters (to June 30, 2026) (TIKR)

And it's paying more to borrow. Steve Eisman, of The Big Short fame, said on The Real Eisman Playbook that CoreWeave's debt was repriced weeks ago from a yield of 9% to 15%. "At a cost of debt of 15%, building AI data centers becomes prohibitively expensive," he said.

title: Microsoft reportedly winds down Oracle AI infrastructure contract
detail:
Microsoft reportedly winds down Oracle AI infrastructure contract
The overall monetary value of the deal was not revealed. Credit: bluestork / Shutterstock.com · Verdict · bluestork / Shutterstock.com
Shubhendu Vimal
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 7:33 AM CST 2 min read
MSFT
ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Microsoft is reportedly scaling back an arrangement to lease AI computing capacity from Oracle following a choice not to extend the agreement, Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed sources.

Originally announced in 2023, the partnership provided Microsoft with access to Oracle servers to operate an AI-supported edition of its Bing search engine.

Over recent months, Microsoft has started decommissioning the leased infrastructure.

The hardware had diminished in usefulness to Microsoft over time as it ceased to satisfy the organisation's technical specifications, with the Oracle systems utilising previous-generation Nvidia processors.

The overall monetary value of the deal was not revealed.

An Oracle representative cited in the report stated that demand for the vendor's AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation graphics processing units (GPUs).

In September, Oracle reported that it was extending agreements for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium over original contract prices.

Oracle's cloud unit has expanded substantially since 2023 on the back of major AI agreements with clients such as OpenAI and Meta Platforms, yielding $18bn in revenue for the year ending May 2026.

However, increased capital expenditures have resulted in negative free cash flow for Oracle, drawing attention from investors.

The non-renewal takes place alongside a broader review by Microsoft of billions of dollars allocated to outside cloud partnerships.

To maintain its AI activities, the software provider had committed upwards of $80bn to lease capacity from external and "neocloud" vendors, including CoreWeave, Nscale, and Nebius.

However, executive management has experienced growing frustration over high expenditure and schedule delays across these providers.

Consequently, Microsoft has implemented stricter monitoring of its data centre initiatives, withdrawn from developments viewed as risky, and commenced internal discussions concerning whether to contract further neocloud capacity.

Late last month, Microsoft also announced a voluntary buyout programme covering approximately 60,000 staff – representing upwards of a quarter of its international workforce – to curb expenses and back ongoing capital deployment in AI.

"Microsoft reportedly winds down Oracle AI infrastructure contract" was originally created and published by Verdict, a GlobalData owned brand.
